panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: This panel shows pediatric patients exhibiting multiple characteristic dysmorphic features associated with alpha-mannosidosis, including macrocephaly, short neck, and facial coarse features, based on caption and clinical description. B: This panel documents a later presentation of the disease in children, showing signs of muscular atrophy in the hands, which is a known clinical finding in alpha-mannosidosis. C: The panel shows anadult patient whose facial morphology is consistent with the reported case of alpha-mannosidosis.

panels.figure_caption: Facial features in alpha-mannosidosis. A. Twins aged 18 Months. Note enlarged head, short neck, rounded eyebrows, saddle nose, and prominent forehead. B. Same twins aged 8 years. Note slight muscular atrophy of the hands. C. Boy, aged 27. Note: Hearing aid.
in_text_mentions: Facial traits may be subtle, but independent of race and background genetics, all patients have some degree of coarse Hurler-like features. This is classically a large head with prominent forehead, rounded eyebrows, flattened nasal bridge, macroglossia, widely spaced teeth, and prognathism. The neck is usually short (Fig 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Panel A is a radiograph showing calvarial thickening and macrocephaly, consistent with alpha-mannosidosis. B: Panel B is a radiograph showing signs of generalized skeletal dysplasia (dysostosis multiplex) in the pelvis. C: Panel C is a radiograph of the ribs showing changes associated with generalized skeletal dysplasia. D: Panel D is a radiograph showing characteristic anterior vertebral beaking, a manifestation of dysostosis multiplex. E: Panel E is a radiograph showing characteristic bone shape abnormalities (bullet-shaped phalanges) indicative of dysostosis multiplex. F: Panel F is an MRI showing neurological findings (Prominent Virchow-Robin spaces) within the context of alpha-mannosidosis, although not directly classified under existing findings keys. G: Panel G is an MRI showing cerebellar atrophy, a neurological complication of alpha-mannosidosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Panel A shows a child with a shield chest and mild carinatum deformity, specific skeletal features of alpha-mannosidosis. B: Panel B shows a child with claw hands and swine neck/foot deformities, consistent with alpha-mannosidosis. C: Panel C shows a child with foot deformity consistent with alpha-mannosidosis. D: Panel D shows siblings with dysmorphic facies, including prominent forehead and prognathism, characteristic of alpha-mannosidosis. E: Panel E shows features in siblings, including genu valgum, macrocephaly, and kyphotic deformity, all consistent with alpha-mannosidosis. F: Panel F illustrates severe features of alpha-mannosidosis, including facial dysmorphology, muscle wasting, and upper limb joint deformities/dystonia.

in_text_mentions: Upon physical examination, the patient exhibited dysmorphic features characterized by coarse facial characteristics such as frontal bossing, supra-orbital bridge prominence, thick eyebrows, a bulbous nose, and thick lips. Her head circumference was 51 cm (70-90th percentile), and her weight was 27 kg (90th percentile). While the vital signs were unremarkable, the skeletal survey displayed evidence of dysostosis multiplex, multilevel lumbar fusion, vertebral anomalies, and S-shaped scoliotic thoracolumbar deformity (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: tient showed unremarkable findings on physical examination, normal developmental milestones, and normal range of motion. The skeletal survey showed absent pneumatization and hypoplastic appearance of the maxillary antra, reduced pneumatization of the mastoid air cells, and hypoplastic frontal sinus. Additionally, there were thickened frontal and occipital bones of the skull. The odontoid process was hypoplastic, with a tendency for atlantoaxial subluxation, and there was potential anterior breaking of lumbar vertebral bodies. A mild widening of the short bones in the hand was noted (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: n and, like the same complication in Gaucher disease, may be treated with epiphyseal arthrodesis at a young age before the epiphyseal lineation of the knee is closed [23]. Over time, from the second till the fourth decade of life the patients may develop destructive polyarthropathy, especially coxarthrosis (Fig 3), but also gonarthrosis [24,25]. These are often so serious that orthopedic corrections are needed [26]. Patellar bilateral dislocation and severe synovial hypertrophy have also been described along with Charcot elbow and bilateral hip and elbow avascular necrosis in one patient [27].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: The panel is a radiographic image of a 3.5-year-old showing coronal view of the skull exhibiting classic features of alpha-mannosidosis. B: The panel is a radiographic image of a 3.5-year-old showing sagittal view of the skull exhibiting classic features of alpha-mannosidosis. C: The panel shows thickened ribs, a skeletal abnormality associated with alpha-mannosidosis. D: The panel shows a fusion defect in the L5 vertebrae, which is an osteoskeletal abnormality associated with alpha-mannosidosis. E: The panel displays osseous abnormalities of the long bones, specifically thickening and shortening, characteristic of alpha-mannosidosis. F: The panel shows metaphyseal widening, another documented skeletal abnormality of alpha-mannosidosis.
panels.attribution_text: Bonilla Fornes et al. Alpha-Mannosidosis in a 3.5-Year-Old Girl: A Case Report.. Clinical case reports 2026. doi:10.1002/ccr3.73276. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Bone examination in a patient aged 3.5 years. (A, B) Coronal and sagittal images showing copper beaten skull and cranial vault thickening. (C) Thick ribs, sagittal view. (D) Fusion defect on posterior arch of L5. (E, F) Slightly thickened short bones in limbs and widening in metaphyses.
in_text_mentions: Total skeletal radiography (Figure 1) revealed a thick cranial vault with prominent convolutional markings (copper beaten skull) (Figure 1A,B), thick ribs (Figure 1C), posterior arch fusion defect at L5 (Figure 1D), shortening and thickening of the long bones, and slight metaphyseal widening (Figure 1E,F).

Osteo‐skeletal abnormalities in alpha‐mannosidosis include multiple dysostoses, genu valgum, kyphosis, scoliosis, asymptomatic osteopenia, sclerotic bone lesions, sternal deformities, hip dysplasia, cranial thickening, and malformed vertebrae [1, 6]. In the present case, the main skeletal abnormalities were shortening of long bones and slight metaphyseal widening of the metaphysis (Figure 1E,F).
